title: Entry points: Main and top-level statements
hook: A process needs one entry point. You either write `static Main` or you put statements at the top of one file and the compiler synthesizes Main. Two files with top-level statements do not compile.

sections.heading: Main versus top-level statements
sections.prose: `dotnet new console` emits top-level statements: executable lines with no class wrapper. The compiler generates a Program class and a Main-like entry point. You still get `args` as a `string[]` in scope, and you can `await` at the top level (that synthesizes an async Main — details in the async module). The classic form is `static void Main(string[] args)` or `static int Main` / `static Task<int> Main`. Both styles work in project-based and file-based apps. Only one file in a compilation may contain top-level statements. Worker hosts (generic host, Lambda function handler) often hide Main inside the framework; your “entry” is then a handler method, but the process still started at Main.

snippets.label: Top-level args versus explicit Main
snippets.explanation: Return codes from Main become the process exit code. Top-level `return` of an int does the same. Do not put a second top-level file in the same project.

interviewTakeaways: Exactly one entry point per executable compilation.
Top-level statements are syntactic sugar for a synthesized Main, not a different runtime model.
`args` is the process argument vector, same idea as `process.argv.slice(2)` but typed as `string[]`.
commonPitfalls: Two Program.cs files both with top-level statements after a copy-paste.
Looking for `Main` in a new template and concluding the app has no entry point.
Forgetting that `await` at top-level changes the synthesized signature to async Main.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node runs the file you pass to `node`. C# always compiles to an entry method. `args` is argv without the runtime path prefix Node includes.
